question.problem: Given that $L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ for $s>0$, find $L\{u(t-11)({t}^{2}-2t+5)\},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.
question.worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then

$$
L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-as}\,L\{g(t+a)\},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0},
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
L\{u(t-11)({t}^{2}-2t+5)\}.
$$

Therefore, $a=11,$ and we have 

$$
L\{u(t-11)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-11s}\,L\{g(t+11)\},
$$

where $g(t)={t}^{2}-2t+5.$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+11) & =(t+11)^{2}-2(t+11)+5 \\  & ={t}^{2}+22t+121\,-\,2t-22\,+\,5 \\  & ={t}^{2}+20t+104.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L\{{t}^{n}\}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ and $L\{1\}=\frac{1}{s}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t+11)\} & =L\{{t}^{2}+20t+104\} \\  & =L\{{t}^{2}\}+20L\{t\}+104L\{1\} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+20\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+104\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{20}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{104}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u(t-11)\,g(t)\} & ={e}^{-11s}\,L\{g(t+11)\} \\  & ={e}^{-11s}(\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{20}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{104}{s}).\end{aligned}
$$
